newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU, Germany at odds over state subsidies.
newsitem.headline: EU, Germany at odds over state subsidies.

text.p: The European Commission, determined to curb German subsidies to businesses, has indicated it will not allow Germany to implement a regional aid plan if support to the rich west is not reduced.

A Commission official said that European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert had told a German parliament delegation that too much money was being channeled to the former west Germany, which includes some of Europe's richest regions.

At issue is a new German plan to support regional development which was recently submitted to the Commission for clearance. Regional aid is financed equally by the EU coffers and national authorities.
The official quoted Van Miert as telling the Bundestag delegation on Monday that he could "live" with the proposals regarding eastern Germany, including Berlin.
But he would press for a reduction of the level of aid to the west.
"The plan must not provide for an increase on the west German side," one official said, adding that it was not even sure whether the Commission would accept the maintenance of the status quo.
It is generally accepted that regional aid must progressively decrease in the European Union as its poorer regions slowly catch up with their richer neighbours.

In Germany, however, the opposite is happening. Because eastern industries receive an increasing amount of state and local aid, their western rivals also step up pressure to get a larger slice of the state support.
The German proposal would benefit 22 percent of the population in the west as oposed to 20.8 percent previously, Commission sources said.

The Commission is increasingly determined to force a reduction in German subsidies, as highlighted by recent disputes over aid to Volkswagen, heavy machinery firm SKET and the country's largest shipyard Bremer Vulkan.
But it faces strong resistance, mainly from the local state authorities which argue they should be allowed to help their industry overcome the damage caused by decades of communist rule.
This contrasts with the criticism, notably by the German Federal Cartel Office, that the Commission is not tough enough in ensuring fair and efective competition.
It also marks a departure from Bonn's traditionally strict respect of the EU rules and authority.
"The call for more discipline regarding state aid is no longer heard in Germany," the official close to Van Miert said.
"There must be a referee (to control state aid) and we must accept that referee."
